modern: Was it so even in the beginning? Did light and darkness divide the realm of time on the very first day? Then it’s little wonder if my circumstances change too, from the sunshine of prosperity to the midnight of hardship. It won’t always be the blaze of noon, even in the things of my soul. At times I must expect to mourn the loss of my former joys and to seek my Beloved in the night. Nor am I alone in this, for all the Lord’s dear ones have had to sing the mixed song of judgment and mercy, of trial and deliverance, of mourning and delight. It is one of the arrangements of God’s providence that day and night won’t cease, in the spiritual creation or the natural one, until we reach the land of which it is written, “there is no night there.” What our heavenly Father ordains is wise and good.

What, then, is best for you to do, my soul? First, learn *to be content* with this divine order, and be willing, like Job, to receive evil from the hand of the Lord as well as good. Next, study to *make the outgoings of the morning and the evening to rejoice*. Praise the Lord for the sun of joy when it rises, and for the gloom of evening as it falls. There is beauty in both sunrise and sunset; sing of it, and glorify the Lord. Like the nightingale, pour out your song at every hour. *Believe that the night is as useful as the day.* The dews of grace fall heavily in the night of sorrow. The stars of promise shine out gloriously in the darkness of grief. *Keep on with your service* through every change. If your watchword in the day is *work*, at night exchange it for *watch*. Every hour has its duty: keep on in your calling as the Lord’s servant until he suddenly appears in his glory. My soul, your evening of old age and death is drawing near. Don’t dread it, for it is part of the day; and the Lord has said, “I will cover him all the day long.”

modern:
I think I see, in a vision, a howling wilderness, a great and terrible desert like the Sahara. I see nothing in it to rest the eye. All around me I am wearied by the sight of hot, dry sand, strewn with ten thousand bleaching skeletons of wretched men who died in anguish after losing their way in that pitiless waste. What an appalling sight! How horrible! A sea of sand without a boundary and without an oasis, a cheerless graveyard for a lost and hopeless race!

But look, and wonder! All of a sudden, springing up out of the scorching sand, I see a plant of renown. As it grows it buds, and the bud opens—it is a rose, and beside it a lily bows its modest head. And, miracle of miracles, as the fragrance of those flowers spreads, the wilderness is turned into a fruitful field. All around it blossoms abundantly; the glory of Lebanon is given to it, the splendor of Carmel and Sharon. Don’t call it Sahara any more; call it Paradise. Don’t speak of it any longer as the valley of the shadow of death, for where the skeletons lay bleaching in the sun, look: a resurrection is proclaimed, and up spring the dead, a mighty army, full of immortal life. Jesus is that plant of renown, and his presence makes all things new.

The wonder is no smaller in each person’s salvation. Over there I see you, dear reader: cast out as a newborn baby, unwrapped, unwashed, stained with your own blood, left to be food for beasts of prey. But look—a jewel has been thrown into your arms by a divine hand, and for its sake you have been pitied and cared for by God’s providence. You are washed and cleansed from your filth; you are adopted into heaven’s family; the fair seal of love is on your forehead, and the ring of faithfulness is on your hand. Once an orphan, cast away, you are now a prince to God. Oh, value above everything the matchless power and grace that turns deserts into gardens and makes the barren heart sing for joy.

modern:
If the young man in the Gospel used this title when he spoke to our Lord, how much more fittingly can I address him this way! He really is my Master in both senses: a Master who rules and a Master who teaches. I love to run his errands and to sit at his feet. I am both his servant and his disciple, and I count it my highest honor to bear both characters. If he were to ask me why I call him “*good*,” I would have an answer ready. It is true that “there is none good but one, that is, God,” but then he is God, and all the goodness of the Godhead shines out in him.

In my own experience I have found him good—so good, in fact, that all the good I have has come to me through him. He was good to me when I was dead in sin, for he raised me by the power of his Spirit; he has been good to me in all my needs, trials, struggles and sorrows. There could never be a better Master, for his service is freedom and his rule is love. I wish I were one-thousandth as good a servant. When he teaches me as my Rabbi, he is unspeakably good: his teaching is divine, his manner is gracious and stooping, and his spirit is gentleness itself. No error mixes with his instruction. The truth he brings out is pure gold, and all his teaching leads to goodness, making the disciple holy as well as building him up.

Angels find him a good Master and delight to pay him homage at his footstool. The saints of old proved him a good Master, and each of them rejoiced to sing, “I am thy servant, O Lord!” My own humble testimony must certainly say the same. I will bear this witness in front of my friends and neighbors, for perhaps my testimony will lead them to seek my Lord Jesus as their Master. Oh, that they would! They would never regret so wise a step. If they would only take his easy yoke, they would find themselves in such royal service that they would sign up for it forever.

modern:
In every believer’s heart there is a constant struggle between the old nature and the new. The old nature is very active, and loses no chance to use every weapon in its deadly armory against the newborn grace. The new nature, on the other side, is always on the watch to resist and destroy its enemy. Grace within us will use prayer, and faith, and hope, and love to drive out the evil; it takes up the “whole armour of God,” and wrestles hard. These two opposing natures will never stop struggling as long as we are in this world. The battle between “Christian” and “Apollyon” lasted three hours, but the battle between Christian and himself lasted all the way from the Wicket Gate to the river Jordan. The enemy is dug in so securely within us that he can never be driven out while we are in this body.

But although we are hard pressed, and often in a fierce fight, we have an Almighty helper, Jesus, the Captain of our salvation. He is always with us, and he assures us that we will come out of it in the end more than conquerors through him. With help like that, the newborn nature is more than a match for its enemies.

Are you fighting the enemy today? Are Satan, the world and the flesh all against you? Don’t be discouraged or dismayed. Fight on! For God himself is with you; Jehovah Nissi is your banner, and Jehovah Rophi is the healer of your wounds. Don’t be afraid—you will overcome, for who can defeat Omnipotence? Fight on, “looking unto Jesus”; and though the conflict is long and hard, the victory will be sweet and the promised reward glorious.

“From strength to strength go on; Wrestle, and fight, and pray, Tread all the powers of darkness down, And win the well-fought day.”

modern:
Potters weren’t the highest class of workers, but “the king” needed potters, and so they were in royal service, even though the material they worked with was nothing but clay. We too may be busy in the humblest part of the Lord’s work, but it is a great privilege to do anything at all for “the king.” So we will stay in our calling, hoping that, “although we have lien among the pots, yet shall we be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold.”

The text tells us of those who *dwelt among plants and hedges*, with rough country work to do, hedging and ditching. They may have wanted to live in the city, in the middle of its life, society and refinement, but they kept to their appointed places, for they too were doing the king’s work. Where we live is fixed for us, and we’re not to move away from it on a whim, but to try to serve the Lord there by being a blessing to the people around us.

These potters and gardeners had *royal company*, for they lived “with the king,” and although they were among hedges and plants, they lived with the king *there*. No lawful place and no honest work, however lowly, can shut us out from fellowship with our divine Lord. When we visit hovels, crowded lodging houses, workhouses or jails, we can go *with the king*. In every work of faith we can count on Jesus’ company. It is when we are doing his work that we can count on his smile.

You unknown workers, busy for your Lord among the dirt and misery of the poorest of the poor, take heart! Jewels have been found on dunghills before now, clay pots have been filled with heavenly treasure, and worthless weeds have been turned into precious flowers. Live with the King for his work, and when he writes his chronicles, your name will be recorded.

modern:
Jesus is the great teacher of a lowly heart. We need to learn from him every day. See the Master taking a towel and washing his disciples’ feet! Follower of Christ, won’t you humble yourself? See him as the Servant of servants, and surely you can’t be proud! Isn’t this sentence the summary of his whole life story: “He humbled himself”? Wasn’t he always, on earth, stripping off one robe of honor after another, until, naked, he was fastened to the cross? And there, didn’t he empty out his inmost self, pouring out his lifeblood, giving himself up for us all, until they laid him penniless in a borrowed grave? How low our dear Redeemer was brought! How then can we be proud?

Stand at the foot of the cross and count the purple drops that have washed you clean. See the crown of thorns; look at his scourged shoulders, still gushing with crimson streams; see his hands and feet given up to the rough iron, and his whole self to mockery and scorn. See the bitterness, the pangs and the agony of inward grief, showing in his outward frame. Hear the piercing cry, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” If you don’t lie flat on the ground before that cross, you have never seen it; if you aren’t humbled in the presence of Jesus, you don’t know him. You were so lost that nothing could save you but the sacrifice of God’s only Son. Think of that, and as Jesus stooped for you, bow yourself low at his feet.

A sense of Christ’s amazing love for us does more to humble us than even an awareness of our own guilt. May the Lord bring us to Calvary in our thoughts; then we will no longer stand like the pompous man of pride, but will take the humble place of one who loves much because much has been forgiven. Pride can’t live beneath the cross. Let’s sit there and learn our lesson, and then get up and put it into practice.

modern:
How sweet it is to see the Savior in fellowship with his own dear people! There can be nothing more delightful than to be led by the Divine Spirit into this fertile field of delight. Let the mind think for a moment about the history of the Redeemer’s love, and a thousand delightful acts of affection will come to mind. Every one of them was meant to weave the heart into Christ, and to twine the thoughts and feelings of the renewed soul together with the mind of Jesus. When we meditate on this amazing love, and see the all-glorious Kinsman of the church endowing her with all his ancient wealth, our souls may well faint for joy. Who could bear such a weight of love? Even the partial sense of it that the Holy Spirit is sometimes pleased to give is more than the soul can hold; how overwhelming a complete view of it must be!

When the soul has the understanding to see all the Savior’s gifts, the wisdom to value them, and the time to meditate on them, as the world to come will give us, then we will have fellowship with Jesus more closely than we do now. But who can imagine the sweetness of that fellowship? It must be one of the things that have not entered into the heart of man, but which God has prepared for those who love him. Oh, to burst open the doors of our Joseph’s granaries and see the plenty he has stored up for us! It will overwhelm us with love. By faith we see, as in a glass darkly, the reflected image of his boundless treasures; but when we actually see the heavenly things themselves, with our own eyes, how deep the stream of fellowship our souls will bathe in! Until then, our loudest songs will be kept for our loving benefactor, Jesus Christ our Lord, whose love for us is wonderful, passing the love of women.

modern:
We have seen our dear Lord in the days of his flesh, humiliated and deeply troubled; for he was “despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.” He whose brightness is like the morning wore the sackcloth of sorrow as his daily clothes; shame was his cloak, and disgrace was his robe. But now, since he has triumphed over all the powers of darkness on the bloody tree, our faith sees our King coming back from Edom with dyed garments, robed in the splendor of victory. How glorious he must have looked to the seraphs when a cloud took him out of mortal sight and he ascended into heaven! Now he wears the glory he had with God before the world began, and yet another glory above it all—the glory he has well earned in the fight against sin, death and hell. As victor he wears the shining crown.

Listen to the song swelling high! It is a new and sweeter song: “Worthy is the Lamb that was slain, for he hath redeemed us unto God by his blood!” He wears the glory of an Intercessor who can never fail, of a Prince who can never be defeated, of a Conqueror who has overcome every enemy, of a Lord who has the heart’s loyalty of every subject. Jesus wears all the glory that the splendor of heaven can give him, all that ten thousand times ten thousand angels can bring him. Stretch your imagination as far as it will go, and you still can’t picture his surpassing greatness. Yet there will be a further showing of it when he comes down from heaven in great power with all the holy angels—“Then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory.” Oh, the splendor of that glory! It will fill his people’s hearts with rapture. Nor is this the end, for eternity will sound his praise: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever!”

Reader, if you want to rejoice in Christ’s glory hereafter, he must be glorious in your eyes now. *Is he?*

modern:
Noah was shut in, away from the whole world, by the hand of divine love. The door of God’s electing purpose stands between us and the world that lies in the wicked one. We are not of the world, just as our Lord Jesus was not of the world. We can’t join in the sin, the frivolity and the pursuits of the crowd; we can’t play in the streets of Vanity Fair with the children of darkness, for our heavenly Father has shut us in.

Noah was shut in *with his God*. “Come thou into the ark,” was the Lord’s invitation, and by it he clearly showed that he himself meant to live in the ark with his servant and his family. In the same way, all the chosen live in God and God in them. Happy people, to be enclosed in the same circle that holds God in the Trinity of his persons, Father, Son and Spirit! Let’s never be deaf to that gracious call, “Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee, and hide thyself as it were for a little moment until the indignation be overpast.”

Noah was shut in so that *no evil could reach him*. The floods only lifted him toward heaven, and the winds only carried him on his way. Outside the ark everything was ruin, but inside all was rest and peace. Without Christ we perish, but in Christ Jesus there is perfect safety.

Noah was shut in so that *he could not even want to come out*, and those who are in Christ Jesus are in him forever. They will go out no more, ever, for eternal faithfulness has shut them in, and the malice of hell can’t drag them out. The Prince of the house of David shuts, and no one opens. And when, in the last days, as Master of the house, he gets up and shuts the door, it will be useless for mere professors to knock and cry, “Lord, Lord, open to us,” for the same door that shuts in the wise virgins will shut out the foolish forever. Lord, shut me in by your grace.

modern:
The distinguishing mark of a Christian is his confidence in the love of Christ, and his giving his heart to Christ in return. First, faith sets her seal on the man by enabling his soul to say with the apostle, “Christ loved me and gave himself for me.” Then love adds the countersign, and stamps gratitude and love to Jesus on the heart in return. “We love him because he first loved us.”

In those great old days, the heroic age of the Christian religion, this double mark could be clearly seen in all believers in Jesus. They were people who knew the love of Christ and leaned on it, the way a man leans on a staff he has tested and found trustworthy. The love they felt for the Lord wasn’t a quiet feeling hidden away in the secret room of their souls, which they mentioned only in their private meetings when they gathered on the first day of the week and sang hymns in honor of Christ Jesus the crucified. It was a passion with them, so fierce and all-consuming that it showed in everything they did. It spoke in their everyday talk and looked out of their eyes in their most ordinary glances. Love for Jesus was a flame that fed on the very core of their being, and so, by its own force, it burned its way out into the outer man and shone there. Zeal for the glory of King Jesus was the seal and mark of every genuine Christian.

Because they relied on Christ’s love they *dared* much, and because they loved Christ they *did* much, and it is the same now. The children of God are ruled in their inmost powers by love: the love of Christ compels them. They rejoice that divine love is set on them; they feel it poured out in their hearts by the Holy Spirit, who is given to them; and then, out of sheer gratitude, they love the Savior with a pure heart, fervently. My reader, do *you* love him? Before you sleep, give an honest answer to a weighty question!

modern: One cheering word for you, poor lost sinner! You think you mustn’t come to God because you are vile. Well, there isn’t a saint living on earth who hasn’t been made to feel that he is vile. If Job and Isaiah and Paul all had to say, “I am vile,” oh, poor sinner, will you be ashamed to join in the same confession? If God’s grace doesn’t root out all sin from the believer, how do you hope to do it yourself? And if God loves his people while they are still vile, do you think your vileness will stop him loving you? Believe on Jesus, you outcast from the world’s society! Jesus calls *you*, and people just like you.

Even now, say, “You died for sinners; I am a sinner, Lord Jesus; sprinkle your blood on me.” If you will confess your sin, you will find pardon. If now, with all your heart, you will say, “I am vile, wash me,” you will be washed now. If the Holy Spirit enables you to cry from your heart

you will get up from reading this morning’s portion with all your sins forgiven. Though you woke this morning with every sin anyone has ever committed on your head, you will rest tonight accepted in the Beloved. Though you were once degraded by the rags of sin, you will be dressed in a robe of righteousness and appear as white as the angels. For “now”—take note of it—“*Now* is the accepted time.” “If thou believest on him who justifieth the ungodly thou art saved.” Oh, may the Holy Spirit give you saving faith in him who receives the vilest!

modern:
We have here *a personal claim*, and one that *needs proof*. The apostle knew that *his* claim was beyond dispute, but many people who have no right to the title still claim to belong to the Israel of God. If we are confidently declaring, “So am I also an Israelite,” let’s say it only after searching our hearts as in the presence of God. But if we can show that we are following Jesus, if we can say from the heart, “I trust him wholly, trust him only, trust him simply, trust him now, and trust him ever,” then the place God’s saints hold belongs to us. All their joys are ours. We may be the very least in Israel, “less than the least of all saints,” yet since God’s mercies belong to the saints *as saints*, and not as advanced saints or well-taught saints, we can put in our plea and say, “Are they Israelites? so am I; therefore the promises are mine, grace is mine, glory will be mine.” Rightly made, the claim will bring untold comfort.

When God’s people are rejoicing that they are his, what happiness if we can say, “*So am I*!” When they speak of being pardoned, and justified, and accepted in the Beloved, how joyful to answer, “Through the grace of God, *so am I*.” But this claim brings not only its joys and privileges but also its conditions and duties. We must share with God’s people in cloud as well as in sunshine. When we hear them spoken of with contempt and ridicule for being Christians, we must step boldly forward and say, “So am I.” When we see them working for Christ, giving their time, their talent, their whole heart to Jesus, we must be able to say, “So do I.” Oh, let’s prove our gratitude by our devotion, and live as people who, having claimed a privilege, are willing to take on the responsibility that comes with it.

modern:
You have good reason to “hate evil,” for just think what harm it has already done you. Oh, what a world of mischief sin has brought into your heart! Sin blinded you, so that you couldn’t see the beauty of the Savior; it made you deaf, so that you couldn’t hear the Redeemer’s tender invitations. Sin turned your feet into the way of death and poured poison into the very fountain of your being. It tainted your heart and made it “deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked.” Oh, what a creature you were when evil had done its worst with you, before God’s grace stepped in! You were an heir of wrath, just like the others; you used to “run with the multitude to do evil.” All of us were like that; but Paul reminds us, “but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”

We have good reason indeed to hate evil when we look back and trace its deadly work. Evil did us such harm that our souls would have been lost if almighty love had not stepped in to redeem us. Even now it is an active enemy, always watching to hurt us and drag us down to ruin. So “hate evil,” Christians, unless you want trouble. If you would like to strew your path with thorns and plant nettles in the pillow of your deathbed, then neglect to “hate evil”; but if you want to live a happy life and die a peaceful death, then walk in all the ways of holiness, hating evil right to the end. If you truly love your Savior and want to honor him, then “hate evil.” We know of no cure for a Christian’s love of evil like plenty of close fellowship with the Lord Jesus. Spend much time with him, and you can’t possibly be at peace with sin.

modern:
If you want to see souls converted, if you want to hear the cry that “the kingdoms of this world have become the kingdoms of our Lord”; if you want to set crowns on the Savior’s head and see his throne lifted high, then be filled with zeal. For, under God, the world will be converted through the zeal of the church. Every grace will do great deeds, but zeal will be first. Prudence, knowledge, patience and courage will follow in their places, but zeal must lead the way. It isn’t the extent of your knowledge, useful as that is; it isn’t the extent of your talent, though that’s not to be despised; it is your zeal that will do great things.

This zeal is the fruit of the Holy Spirit: it draws its life from *the continued work* of the Holy Spirit in the soul. If our inner life dwindles, if our heart beats slowly toward God, we won’t know zeal. But if all is strong and vigorous within, then we can’t help feeling a loving longing to see the kingdom of Christ come and his will done on earth as it is in heaven.

A deep *sense of gratitude* will feed Christian zeal. When we look back to the hole of the pit we were dug out of, we find plenty of reason to spend and be spent for God. Zeal is also stirred by *the thought of the eternal future*. It looks with tearful eyes down at the flames of hell, and it can’t sleep; it looks up with eager eyes at the glories of heaven, and it can’t help rousing itself. It feels that time is short compared with the work to be done, and so it gives everything it has to the cause of its Lord. And it is always strengthened by *the memory of Christ’s example*. He was clothed with zeal as with a cloak. How swiftly the chariot wheels of duty rolled with him! He never lingered along the way. Let’s prove we are his disciples by showing the same spirit of zeal.

modern:
Warrior fighting under the banner of the Lord Jesus, read this verse with holy joy, for as it was in the old days so it is now: if the war is of God, the victory is sure. The sons of Reuben, the Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh could barely muster forty-five thousand fighting men, and yet in their war with the Hagarites they killed “men, an hundred thousand,” “for they cried to God in the battle, and he was entreated of them, because they put their trust in him.” The Lord doesn’t save by many or by few. Our part is to go out in Jehovah’s name, even if we are only a handful, for the Lord of Hosts is with us as our Captain. They didn’t neglect shield and sword and bow, but they didn’t put their trust in those weapons either. We must use every proper means, but our confidence must rest in the Lord alone, for he is the sword and the shield of his people. The great reason for their extraordinary success was that “the war was of God.”

Dear reader, when you fight sin outside you and within, error in teaching or in practice, spiritual wickedness in high places or low places, devils and the devil’s allies, you are waging Jehovah’s war; and unless he himself can be beaten, you needn’t fear defeat. Don’t cower before greater numbers. Don’t shrink from difficulties or impossibilities. Don’t flinch at wounds or death. Strike with the two-edged sword of the Spirit, and the slain will lie in heaps. The battle is the Lord’s, and he will hand his enemies over to us. With steady foot, strong hand, fearless heart and flaming zeal, rush into the fight, and the armies of evil will fly like chaff before the wind.

modern:
God had made Moses a definite promise that for a whole month he would feed the vast crowd in the wilderness with meat. Moses, overtaken by a fit of unbelief, looks at the outward means and can’t see how the promise can be kept. He looked to the creature instead of the Creator. But does the Creator expect the creature to keep his promise for him? No. He who makes the promise always keeps it by his own unaided almighty power. If he speaks, it is done, and done by himself. His promises don’t depend for their fulfillment on the help of man’s puny strength.

We can see straight away the mistake Moses made. And yet how often we do the same! God has promised to supply our needs, and we look to the creature to do what God has promised to do. Then, because we see that the creature is weak and feeble, we give in to unbelief. Why look in that direction at all? Would you go to the North Pole to gather fruit ripened in the sun? Truly, you would act no more foolishly doing that than when you look to the weak for strength, and to the creature to do the Creator’s work.

Let’s put the question, then, on the right footing. The ground of faith isn’t whether the visible means are enough to keep the promise, but the all-sufficiency of the invisible God, who will most surely do as he has said. If, after seeing clearly that the burden lies with the Lord and not with the creature, we still dare to give in to mistrust, God’s question comes home to us with power: “Has the Lord’s hand waxed short?” And in his mercy, may it happen that with the question there flashes into our souls that blessed declaration, “Thou shalt see now whether my word shall come to pass unto thee or not.”

modern:
Some Christians are sadly inclined to *look* on the *dark* side of everything, and to dwell more on what they have gone through than on what God has done for them. Ask them what the Christian life has been like, and they will describe their constant conflicts, their deep afflictions, their sad misfortunes and the sinfulness of their hearts, with hardly a mention of the mercy and help God has given them. But a Christian whose soul is *healthy* will come forward joyfully and say, “I will speak, not about myself, but to the honour of my God. He hath brought me up out of an horrible pit, and out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings: and he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God. The Lord hath done great things for me, whereof I am glad.” A summary of experience like that is the very best any child of God can give.

It’s true that we endure trials, but it’s just as true that we are delivered out of them. It’s true that we have our corruptions, and we know it to our sorrow, but it’s quite as true that we have an all-sufficient Savior, who overcomes these corruptions and frees us from their power. Looking back, it would be wrong to deny that we have been in the Slough of Despond and have crept along the Valley of Humiliation, but it would be equally wicked to forget that we have come *through* them, safely and to our profit. We didn’t stay in them, thanks to our Almighty Helper and Leader, who has brought us “out into a wealthy place.” The deeper our troubles, the louder our thanks to God, who has led us through them all and kept us until now. Our griefs can’t spoil the melody of our praise; we count them as the bass part of our life’s song: “He hath done great things for us, whereof we are glad.”

modern:
The Greek word translated *search* here means a strict, close, careful, inquisitive search, the kind people make when they are looking for gold, or hunters when they are hot on the trail of game. We mustn’t be satisfied with having given a chapter or two a quick reading. With the candle of the Spirit we must deliberately seek out the hidden meaning of the word.

Holy Scripture *needs searching*; much of it can only be learned by careful study. There is milk for babies, but there is also meat for strong men. The rabbis wisely say that a mountain of meaning hangs on every word, yes, on every tittle of Scripture. Tertullian exclaims, “I adore the fulness of the Scriptures.” No one who merely skims the book of God can profit from it; we must dig and mine until we reach the hidden treasure. The door of the word opens only to the key of diligence.

The Scriptures *deserve searching*. They are the writings of God, bearing the divine stamp and seal of approval. Who would dare to treat them lightly? Whoever despises them despises the God who wrote them. God forbid that any of us should leave our Bibles to become swift witnesses against us on the great day of reckoning.

The word of God *will repay searching*. God doesn’t tell us to sift a mountain of chaff with a grain of wheat here and there in it. The Bible is threshed and winnowed grain; we have only to open the granary door and find it. Scripture grows on the student. It is full of surprises. Under the teaching of the Holy Spirit, it glows before the searching eye with the splendor of revelation, like a vast temple paved with beaten gold and roofed with rubies, emeralds and every kind of gem. There is no merchandise like the merchandise of Scripture truth.

Lastly, *the Scriptures reveal Jesus*: “They are they which testify of me.” No more powerful reason can be pressed on Bible readers than this: whoever finds Jesus finds life, heaven, everything. Happy is the one who searches his Bible and discovers his Savior there.

modern:
If God had wanted it so, each of us could have gone to heaven the moment we were converted. It wasn’t absolutely necessary, to prepare us for immortality, that we should stay here. A person can be taken to heaven, and be found fit to share the inheritance of the saints in light, though he has only just believed in Jesus. It’s true that our sanctification is a long, ongoing process, and we won’t be made perfect until we lay aside our bodies and enter within the veil. All the same, if the Lord had wanted to, he could have changed us from imperfection to perfection and taken us to heaven at once.

Why then are we here? Would God keep his children out of paradise a single moment longer than necessary? Why is the army of the living God still on the battlefield, when one charge could win them the victory? Why are his children still wandering here and there through a maze, when a single word from his lips would bring them into the center of their hopes in heaven? The answer is that they are here so that they may “*live unto the Lord*,” and bring others to know his love. We stay on earth as sowers, to scatter good seed; as plowmen, to break up the unplowed ground; as heralds, announcing salvation. We are here as the “salt of the earth,” to be a blessing to the world. We are here to glorify Christ in our daily life. We are here as workers for him, and as “workers together with him.” Let’s make sure our life fulfills its purpose. Let’s live earnest, useful, holy lives, to “the praise of the glory of his grace.” Meanwhile we long to be with him, and every day we sing—

notes.note: “Which hath made us meet to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light” ([[Col.1.12|Colossians 1:12]]).

modern:
Jesus Christ is the Alpha and Omega of the Bible. He is the constant theme of its sacred pages; from first to last they testify of him. At the creation we see him straight away as one of the sacred Trinity. We catch a glimpse of him in the promise of the woman’s seed; we see him pictured in Noah’s ark; we walk with Abraham as he sees the Messiah’s day; we live in the tents of Isaac and Jacob, feeding on the gracious promise; we hear old Israel speaking of Shiloh; and in the many types of the law we find the Redeemer foreshadowed again and again. Prophets and kings, priests and preachers, all look one way. They all stand as the cherubs did over the ark, longing to look within and read the mystery of God’s great propitiation.

Still more plainly in the New Testament, our Lord is the one subject running through it all. It isn’t a gold bar here and there, or gold dust thinly scattered; here you stand on a solid floor of gold, for the whole substance of the New Testament is Jesus crucified, and even its closing sentence is set with the jewel of the Redeemer’s name.

We should always read Scripture in this light. We should think of the word as a mirror that Christ looks down into from heaven; then we, looking into it, see his face reflected as in a glass—darkly, it’s true, but still in a way that blessedly prepares us to see him as we will see him face to face. This book contains Jesus Christ’s letters to us, perfumed with his love. These pages are the garments of our King, and they all smell of myrrh, and aloes, and cassia. Scripture is the royal chariot in which Jesus rides, and it is paved with love for the daughters of Jerusalem. The Scriptures are the swaddling clothes of the holy child Jesus; unroll them and you find your Savior. The very essence of the word of God is Christ.

notes.note: The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending” ([[Rev.1.8|Revelation 1:8]]).

modern:
There is no light in the planet except what comes from the sun, and there is no true love for Jesus in the heart except what comes from the Lord Jesus himself. All our love for God must spring from this overflowing fountain, the infinite love of God. This must always be a great and certain truth: we love him for no other reason than that he first loved us. Our love for him is *the fair child* of his love for us. Anyone may have a cold admiration when studying the works of God, but only God’s Spirit can kindle the warmth of love in the heart. What a wonder that people like us should ever have been brought to love Jesus at all! How marvelous that when we had rebelled against him, he should try to draw us back by showing such amazing love! No, we would never have had a grain of love for God unless it had been sown in us by the sweet seed of his love for us.

Love, then, has the love of God poured out in the heart for its parent. But once it is born of God like this, it must *be fed by God*. Love is a hothouse plant; it won’t flourish naturally in human soil, but must be watered from above. Love for Jesus is a delicate flower, and if it got no food except what could be drawn from the rock of our hearts, it would soon wither. As love comes from heaven, so it must feed on heavenly bread. It can’t survive in the wilderness unless it is fed with manna from on high. Love must feed on love. The very soul and life of our love for God is his love for us.

notes.note: Comes, goes out from.

notes.term: We love him because he first loved us

notes.note: “The love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost” ([[Rom.5.5|Romans 5:5]]). Shed abroad means poured out.
A plant from a warmer country, which won’t grow outdoors in Britain without special care.

modern:
Our Redeemer’s glorious cry, “It is finished,” was the death knell of all the enemies of his people, the breaking of “the arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword, and the battle.” See the hero of Golgotha, using his cross as an anvil and his sufferings as a hammer, smashing to splinters bundle after bundle of our sins, those poisoned “arrows of the bow”; trampling on every charge and destroying every accusation. What glorious blows the mighty Breaker strikes, with a hammer far heavier than the legendary weapon of Thor! How the devilish darts fly to pieces, and the shields of hell are broken like potters’ jars! Look, he draws the dreadful sword of Satan’s power from its sheath of hellish workmanship! He snaps it across his knee, as a man breaks the dry sticks of a bundle of firewood, and throws it into the fire.

Dear reader, no sin of a believer can now be an arrow to wound him fatally, and no condemnation can now be a sword to kill him, for Christ bore the punishment of our sin; our blessed Substitute and Surety made a full atonement for all our wrongdoing. Who accuses now? Who condemns now? Christ has died, yes, and more than that, has risen again. Jesus has emptied the quivers of hell, quenched every fiery dart, and broken off the head of every arrow of wrath. The ground is strewn with the splinters and remains of the weapons of hell’s warfare, and we see them only to remind us of our former danger and our great deliverance. Sin has no more dominion over us. Jesus has made an end of it and put it away forever. You enemy, your destructions have come to a final end. Talk of all the wonderful works of the Lord, all you who mention his name; don’t keep silent, by day or when the sun goes down. Bless the Lord, O my soul.

notes.note: Jesus’ cry from the cross ([[John.19.30|John 19:30]]).

modern:
It is good to weigh ourselves often in the scales of God’s Word. You will find it a holy exercise to read one of David’s psalms and, as you meditate on each verse, to ask yourself, “Can I say this? Have I felt as David felt? Has my heart ever been broken over sin, as his was when he wrote his psalms of repentance? Has my soul been full of real confidence in the hour of difficulty, as his was when he sang of God’s mercies in the cave of Adullam, or in the strongholds of Engedi? Do I take the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord?”

Then turn to the life of Christ, and as you read, ask yourself how far you are shaped into his likeness. Try to discover whether you have the meekness, the humility, the lovely spirit that he constantly taught and showed. Then take the letters of the apostles and see whether you can go along with the apostle in what he said of his own experience. Have you ever cried out as he did—“O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” Have you ever felt his lowliness? Have you seemed to yourself the chief of sinners, and less than the least of all saints? Have you known anything of his devotion? Could you join him and say, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain”?

If we read God’s Word like this, as a test of our spiritual condition, we will have good reason to stop many times and say, “Lord, I feel I have never yet been here. Oh, bring me here! Give me true repentance, like this I read of. Give me real faith; give me warmer zeal; set me on fire with more fervent love; grant me the grace of meekness; make me more like Jesus. Don’t let me be ‘found wanting’ any longer when I am weighed in the balances of the sanctuary, or I will be found wanting in the scales of judgment.” “Judge yourselves that ye be not judged.”

modern:
The apostle uses the perfect tense and says, “Who *hath* saved us.” Believers in Christ Jesus *are* saved. They aren’t seen as people in a hopeful condition who may eventually be saved; they *are* saved already. Salvation isn’t a blessing to be enjoyed on our deathbed and to be sung of in a future state above. It is something to be obtained, received, promised and enjoyed now.

The Christian is perfectly saved *in God’s purpose*: God has ordained him to salvation, and that purpose is complete. He is also saved as far as *the price paid for him* goes: “It is finished” was the Savior’s cry before he died. And the believer is perfectly saved *in his covenant head*, for as he fell in Adam, so he lives in Christ.

This complete salvation comes with *a holy calling*. Those whom the Savior saved on the cross are, in due time, effectually called to holiness by the power of God the Holy Spirit. They leave their sins; they try to be like Christ; they choose holiness, not because they are forced to, but under the pressure of a new nature, which leads them to delight in holiness just as naturally as they once delighted in sin. God didn’t choose them or call them because they were holy; he called them so that they might be holy, and holiness is the beauty his workmanship produces in them. The excellent qualities we see in a believer are as much God’s work as the atonement itself.

This brings out very sweetly the fullness of God’s grace. Salvation must be by grace, because the Lord is its author: and what motive but grace could move him to save the guilty? Salvation must be by grace, because the Lord works in such a way that our own righteousness is shut out forever. This is the believer’s privilege—*a present salvation*; and this is the evidence that he is called to it—*a holy life*.

notes.note: The verb form for something done and finished: “hath saved,” not “will save.”

modern:
Jesus says, “take freely.” He wants no payment and no preparation. He looks for no recommendation from our good feelings. If you have no good feelings, but you are willing, you are invited; so come! You have no belief and no repentance? Come to him, and he will give them to you. Come just as you are, and take “Freely,” without money and without price. He gives himself to people in need.

The drinking fountains on our street corners are valuable things, and we can hardly imagine anyone so foolish as to reach for his wallet when he stands in front of one and cry, “I can’t drink, because I haven’t got five pounds in my pocket.” However poor a man is, there is the fountain, and just as he is he may drink from it. Thirsty passers-by, whether they are dressed in workman’s cloth or in fine wool, don’t look for any permit to drink; the fountain’s being there is their permission to take its water freely. Some good friends have generously put the refreshing water there, and we take it and ask no questions.

Perhaps the only people who need to go thirsty along a street where there is a drinking fountain are the fine ladies and gentlemen in their carriages. They are very thirsty, but they can’t think of being so common as to get out and drink. It would lower them, they think, to drink at a public fountain, so they ride by with parched lips. Oh, how many there are who are rich in their own good works and so can’t come to Christ! “I won’t be saved,” they say, “in the same way as the prostitute or the swearer. What! Go to heaven the same way as a chimney sweep? Is there no road to glory except the path that led the thief there? I won’t be saved that way.” Such proud boasters must stay without the living water. But “Whosoever will, let him *take the water of life freely*.”

*“O my God, be not far from me.”*

[[Ps.38.21|Psalm 38:21]]

Here we have two great lessons: what to pray against and what to pray for. The happiest state of a Christian is the holiest state. Just as there is most heat nearest the sun, so there is most happiness nearest to Christ. No Christian enjoys comfort while his eyes are fixed on empty things; he finds no satisfaction unless his soul is made alive in the ways of God. The world may find happiness elsewhere, but he can’t. I don’t blame ungodly people for rushing to their pleasures. Why should I? Let them have their fill. That is all they have to enjoy. A converted wife who despaired of her husband was always very kind to him, for she said, “I fear that this is the only world in which he will be happy, and therefore I have made up my mind to make him as happy as I can in it.” Christians must look for their delights in a higher sphere than the tasteless trivia or sinful pleasures of the world.

Empty pursuits are dangerous to renewed souls. We have heard of a philosopher who fell into a pit while he looked *up* at the stars; but how deeply they fall who look *down*! Their fall is fatal. No Christian is safe when his soul is lazy and his God is far from him. Every Christian is always safe as to the great matter of his standing in Christ, but he isn’t safe as regards his experience of holiness and fellowship with Jesus in this life. Satan doesn’t often attack a Christian who is living close to God. It is when the Christian wanders from his God, grows spiritually starved and tries to feed on empty things that the devil sees his opportunity. He may sometimes stand toe to toe with the child of God who is busy in his Master’s service, but the battle is usually short. Whoever slips as he goes down into the Valley of Humiliation invites Apollyon to attack him every time he takes a false step. Oh, for grace to walk humbly with our God!

modern:
The teaching of these words must seem very surprising to people who are strangers to living faith, but to the sincere believer it only presses home a truth he already knows. The believer’s life is described here as a *delight* in God, and this assures us of the great fact that true religion overflows with happiness and joy. Ungodly people and those who only claim to be Christians never see religion as a joyful thing. To them it is service, duty or necessity, but never pleasure or delight. If they pay attention to religion at all, it is either so that they can gain by it, or else because they don’t dare do otherwise. The thought of *delight* in religion is so strange to most people that no two words in their language stand further apart than “holiness” and “delight.”

But believers who know Christ understand that delight and faith are so blessedly joined that the gates of hell can’t separate them. Those who love God with all their hearts find that his ways are ways of pleasantness, and all his paths are peace. The saints discover such joys, such brimming delights, such overflowing happiness in their Lord, that far from serving him out of habit, they would follow him even if all the world threw out his name as evil. We don’t fear God because we are forced to. Our faith is no chain, our profession is no slavery; we aren’t dragged to holiness or driven to duty. No, our godliness is our pleasure, our hope is our happiness, our duty is our delight.
Delight and true religion are as joined as root and flower, as inseparable as truth and certainty. They are, in fact, two precious jewels glittering side by side in a setting of gold.

modern:
A deep sense and a clear sight of sin, of how hateful it is and the punishment it deserves, should make us lie low before the throne. We have sinned as Christians. How sad that it should be so! Favored as we have been, we have still been ungrateful; privileged beyond most, we haven’t borne fruit to match. Who is there, even if he has long been engaged in the Christian warfare, who won’t blush when he looks back on the past? As for our days before we were born again, may they be forgiven and forgotten. But since then, though we haven’t sinned as we did before, we have sinned against light and against love: light that has really entered our minds, and love we have rejoiced in. Oh, the outrage of a pardoned soul’s sin! An unpardoned sinner sins cheaply compared with the sin of one of God’s own chosen ones, who has had fellowship with Christ and leaned his head on Jesus’ chest.

Look at David! Many will talk about his sin, but I beg you, look at his repentance, and hear his broken bones as each one moans out its mournful confession! See his tears as they fall on the ground, and the deep sighs that go with the softened music of his harp! We have gone wrong; let’s seek, then, the spirit of repentance. Look, again, at Peter! We talk a lot about Peter’s denying his Master. Remember, it is written, “He wept bitterly.” Have *we* no denials of our Lord to mourn with tears? Sadly, these sins of ours, before and after conversion, would send us to the place of unquenchable fire if it weren’t for the sovereign mercy that has made us different, snatching us like burning sticks from the fire. My soul, bow down under a sense of your natural sinfulness, and worship your God. Marvel at the grace that saves you, the mercy that spares you, the love that pardons you!

modern: It was far beyond the power of nature, and even against its laws, that the aged Sarah should be honored with a son. In the same way, it is beyond all ordinary rules that I, a poor, helpless, ruined sinner, should find grace to carry the indwelling Spirit of the Lord Jesus in my soul. I once despaired, and I had good reason to, for my nature was as dry and withered and barren and cursed as a howling wilderness. Yet even I have been made to bear fruit to holiness. Well may my mouth be filled with joyful laughter, because of the extraordinary, surprising grace I have received from the Lord, for I have found Jesus, the promised seed, and he is mine forever. Today I will lift up psalms of triumph to the Lord who has remembered my low condition, for “my heart rejoiceth in the Lord; mine horn is exalted in the Lord; my mouth is enlarged over mine enemies, because I rejoice in thy salvation.”

I want everyone who hears of my great deliverance from hell, and of the blessed visit from on high I have received, to laugh for joy with me. I would surprise my family with my abundant peace; I would delight my friends with my ever-growing happiness; I would build up the church with my grateful testimony; and I would even impress the world with the cheerfulness of my everyday life. Bunyan tells us that Mercy laughed in her sleep, and no wonder, when she dreamed of Jesus. My joy won’t fall short of hers while my Beloved is the subject of my daily thoughts. The Lord Jesus is a deep sea of joy: my soul will dive into it and be swallowed up in the delights of his company. Sarah looked at her Isaac and laughed with overflowing delight, and all her friends laughed with her. And you, my soul, look at your Jesus, and call on heaven and earth to join in your inexpressible joy.

modern:
Jesus is the keeper of the gates of paradise, and before every believing soul he sets an open door that no man or devil will be able to close. What joy it will be to find that faith in him is the golden key to the everlasting doors! My soul, are you carrying this key close to your heart, or are you trusting some deceitful lock-pick that will fail you in the end?

Listen to this parable of the preacher, and remember it. The great King has made a banquet, and he has announced to all the world that no one will come in except those who bring with them the fairest flower that blooms. Human spirits come up to the gate by the thousands, each bringing the flower he thinks the queen of the garden; but they are driven from the royal presence in crowds and never enter the festive halls. Some carry in their hand the deadly nightshade of superstition, or the gaudy poppies of Rome, or the hemlock of self-righteousness; but these aren’t dear to the King, and those who carry them are shut out of the pearly gates.

My soul, have you gathered the rose of Sharon? Do you always wear the lily of the valley close to your heart? If so, when you come up to the gates of heaven you will know its value, for you have only to show this choicest of flowers and the Porter will open. Not for a moment will he refuse you entry, for to that rose the Porter always opens. With the rose of Sharon in your hand you will find your way right up to the throne of God himself, for heaven itself has nothing more beautiful, and of all the flowers that bloom in paradise there is none that can rival the lily of the valley. My soul, take Calvary’s blood-red rose into your hand by faith; wear it by love; keep it fresh by fellowship; make it your all in all by daily watchfulness; and you will be blessed beyond all bliss, happy beyond a dream. Jesus, be mine forever, my God, my heaven, my all.

modern:
A Christian should never think or speak lightly of unbelief. For a child of God to mistrust God’s love, his truth, his faithfulness, must greatly displease him. How can we ever grieve him by doubting his upholding grace? Christian, it goes against every promise of God’s precious Word that you should ever be forgotten or left to perish. If that could happen, how could he be true who has said, “Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yea, they may forget, yet will I never forget thee.” What would this promise be worth: “The mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but my kindness shall not depart from thee, neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed, saith the Lord that hath mercy on thee”? Where would the truth of Christ’s words be: “I give unto my sheep eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father’s hand”? Where would the doctrines of grace be? They would all be disproved if one child of God were to perish. Where would God’s truthfulness be, his honor, his power, his grace, his covenant, his oath, if any of those for whom Christ has died, and who have put their trust in him, were cast away after all?

Banish those unbelieving fears that so dishonor God. Get up, shake yourself from the dust, and put on your beautiful garments. Remember it is sinful to doubt his Word, in which he has promised you that you will never perish. Let the eternal life within you show itself in confident rejoicing.

modern:
“*The Lord is my light and my salvation*.” Here is personal ownership: “*my light*,” “*my salvation*.” The soul is sure of it, and so it declares it boldly. At the new birth, divine light is poured into the soul as the forerunner of salvation. Where there isn’t enough light to show us our own darkness and make us long for the Lord Jesus, there is no evidence of salvation. After conversion our God is our joy, comfort, guide, teacher, and in every sense our light: he is light within, light around, light reflected from us, and light still to be revealed to us. Notice that it doesn’t say merely that the Lord gives light, but that he is light; nor that he gives salvation, but that he is salvation. So whoever has taken hold of God by faith has every covenant blessing in his possession.

With this settled as a fact, the argument drawn from it is put as a question: “*Whom shall I fear*?” It is a question that answers itself. The powers of darkness aren’t to be feared, for the Lord, our light, destroys them; and we needn’t dread the damnation of hell, for the Lord is our salvation. This is a very different challenge from boastful Goliath’s, for it rests not on the conceited strength of an arm of flesh, but on the real power of the almighty I AM.

“*The Lord is the strength of my life*.” Here is a third glowing title, to show that the writer’s hope was tied with a threefold cord that couldn’t be broken. We may well pile up words of praise where the Lord pours out deeds of grace. Our life draws all its strength from God, and if he is pleased to make us strong, all the schemes of the enemy can’t weaken us. “*Of whom shall I be afraid*?” The bold question looks into the future as well as the present. “If God be for us,” who can be against us, now or in time to come?

modern: *The prayer itself is remarkable*, for it is *short*, but *timely, pithy* and *suggestive*. David mourned how few faithful men were left, and so he lifted up his heart in prayer: when the creature failed, he flew to the Creator. He clearly felt his own weakness, or he wouldn’t have cried for help; but at the same time he honestly meant to do his own part for the cause of truth, for the word “help” makes no sense where we ourselves do nothing. There is a great deal of *directness, clear sight* and *plain speaking* in this two-word request; far more, in fact, than in the long, rambling outpourings of some who profess the faith. The psalmist runs straight to his God with a well-considered prayer. He knows what he is looking for and where to look for it. Lord, teach us to pray in the same blessed way.

*The occasions for using this prayer are frequent*. How suitable it is in the troubles of providence, for tried believers who find every helper failing them! Students in *difficulties of doctrine* can often get help by lifting up this cry, “Help, Lord,” to the Holy Spirit, the great Teacher. Spiritual warriors in *inward conflicts* can send to the throne for reinforcements, and this will be a model for their request. Workers in *heavenly labor* can get grace this way in time of need. Seeking sinners in *doubts and alarms* can offer up the same weighty plea. In fact, in all these cases, times and places, this will meet the need of needy souls. “Help, Lord,” will suit us living and dying, suffering or working, rejoicing or sorrowing. Our help is found in him; let’s not be slow to cry to him.

*The answer to the prayer is certain*, if it is offered sincerely through Jesus. The Lord’s character assures us that he won’t leave his people; his relationship as Father and Husband guarantees us his help; his gift of Jesus is a pledge of every good thing; and his sure promise stands: “Fear not, *I will help thee*.”

modern:
The well of Beer in the wilderness was famous, because it was *the subject of a promise*: “That is the well whereof the Lord spake unto Moses, Gather the people together, and I will give them water.” The people needed water, and their gracious God promised it. We need fresh supplies of heavenly grace, and in the covenant the Lord has pledged himself to give everything we need.

Next, the well became *the cause of a song*. Before the water gushed out, cheerful faith prompted the people to sing; and as they saw the crystal spring bubbling up, the music grew more joyful still. In the same way, we who believe God’s promise should rejoice at the prospect of God reviving our souls, and as we experience it our holy joy should overflow. Are we thirsty? Let’s not grumble, but sing. Spiritual thirst is bitter to bear, but we needn’t bear it: the promise points to a well. Let’s take heart and look for it.

Moreover, the well was *the center of prayer*. “Spring up, O well.” What God has undertaken to give, we must ask after, or we show that we have neither desire nor faith. This evening let’s ask that the Scripture we have read and our times of devotion won’t be an empty formality, but a channel of grace to our souls. Oh, that God the Holy Spirit would work in us with all his mighty power, filling us with all the fullness of God!

Lastly, the well was *the object of effort*. “The nobles of the people digged it with their staves.” The Lord wants us to be active in seeking grace. Our staffs are poorly suited to digging in the sand, but we must use them to the utmost of our ability. Prayer mustn’t be neglected; meeting together mustn’t be given up; the ordinances mustn’t be treated lightly. The Lord will give us his peace most generously, but not to the idle. So let’s rouse ourselves to seek him in whom are all our fresh springs.

modern: Jesus the Redeemer is altogether ours, and ours forever. All the *offices* of Christ are held on our behalf. He is king for us, priest for us and prophet for us. Whenever we read a new title of the Redeemer, let’s take him as ours under that name as much as under any other. The shepherd’s staff, the father’s rod, the captain’s sword, the priest’s turban, the prince’s scepter, the prophet’s mantle: all are ours. Jesus has no dignity he won’t use to lift us up, and no privilege he won’t exercise to defend us. His fullness of *Godhead* is our unfailing, inexhaustible treasure-house.

His *manhood* too, which he took on himself for us, is ours in all its perfection. To us our gracious Lord passes on the spotless goodness of a stainless character; to us he gives the merit and power of a devoted life; on us he bestows the reward earned by obedient submission and unceasing service. He makes the unstained garment of his life our covering beauty; the glittering virtues of his character our ornaments and jewels; and the superhuman meekness of his death our boast and glory. He leaves us his manger, to learn from it how God came down to man; and his cross, to teach us how man may go up to God. All his thoughts, feelings, actions, words, miracles and prayers for others were for us. He walked the road of sorrow on our behalf, and has handed over to us, as his heavenly legacy, the full results of all the labors of his life. He is as much ours now as he ever was; and he isn’t ashamed to call himself “*our* Lord Jesus Christ,” though he is the blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings and Lord of lords. Christ everywhere and every way is our Christ, ours forever and ever to enjoy to the full. O my soul, by the power of the Holy Spirit, call him “thy Redeemer” this morning!

modern:
The believer’s heart is Christ’s garden. He bought it with his precious blood, and he comes into it and claims it as his own.

A garden *means separation*. It isn’t the open common; it isn’t a wilderness; it is walled around or hedged in. I wish we could see the wall of separation between the church and the world made wider and stronger. It’s sad to hear Christians saying, “Well, there is no harm in this; there is no harm in that,” and so getting as close to the world as they can. Grace is at a low ebb in a soul that can even ask how far it may go in fitting in with the world.

A garden is *a place of beauty*; it far outshines the wild, uncultivated land. The genuine Christian must try to be more excellent in his life than the best moralist, because Christ’s garden ought to produce the best flowers in all the world. Even the best is poor compared with what Christ deserves; let’s not fob him off with withering, stunted plants. The rarest, richest, choicest lilies and roses ought to bloom in the place Jesus calls his own.

The garden is *a place of growth*. The saints aren’t to stay undeveloped, forever mere buds and blossoms. We should grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Growth should be rapid where Jesus is the Gardener and the Holy Spirit the dew from above.

A garden is *a place of retreat*. In the same way, the Lord Jesus Christ wants us to keep our souls as a place where he can show himself to us as he doesn’t to the world. Oh, that Christians kept more to themselves, and kept their hearts more closely shut up for Christ! We often worry and fuss, like Martha, with much serving, so that we don’t have the room for Christ that Mary had, and we don’t sit at his feet as we should. May the Lord send the sweet showers of his grace to water his garden today.

modern:
How rich the blessings of this day would be if all of us were filled with the Holy Spirit! The results of this sacred filling of the soul could not possibly be overstated. Life, comfort, light, purity, power, peace and many other precious blessings are inseparable from the Spirit’s kindly presence.

As sacred *oil*, he anoints the believer’s head, sets him apart to the priesthood of the saints, and gives him grace to carry out his office rightly. As the only truly purifying *water*, he cleanses us from the power of sin and makes us holy, working in us both to will and to do the Lord’s good pleasure. As the *light*, he first showed us our lost condition, and now he reveals the Lord Jesus to us and in us, and guides us in the way of righteousness. Lit by his pure heavenly ray, we are no longer darkness but light in the Lord. *As fire*, he both burns the impurities out of us and sets our consecrated nature ablaze. He is the sacrificial flame that enables us to offer our whole souls as a living sacrifice to God. As heavenly *dew*, he takes away our barrenness and makes our lives fruitful. Oh, that he would fall on us from above at this early hour! Such morning dew would be a sweet beginning to the day. As the *dove*, with wings of peaceful love, he broods over his church and over the souls of believers, and as a Comforter he drives away the cares and doubts that spoil the peace of his dear ones. He comes down on the chosen as on the Lord at the Jordan, and bears witness that they are God’s children by working in them the spirit of a child, by which they cry, Abba, Father. As the *wind*, he brings the breath of life to men; blowing where he pleases, he does the life-giving work that animates and sustains the spiritual creation. I wish to God that we might feel his presence today and every day!

modern: Surely if there is a happy verse in the Bible, it is this: “My Beloved is mine, and I am his.” It is so peaceful, so full of assurance, so overflowing with happiness and contentment, that it could well have been written by the same hand that wrote the twenty-third Psalm. Yet though the view is extremely fair and lovely—earth can’t show anything to beat it—it isn’t entirely a sunlit landscape. There is a cloud in the sky that casts a shadow over the scene. Listen: “Until the day break, and the shadows flee away.”

There is a word too about the “mountains of Bether,” or, “the mountains of division,” and to our love, anything like division is bitterness. Dear reader, this may be your state of mind right now. You don’t doubt your salvation; you know that Christ is yours; but you aren’t feasting with him. You understand your living share in him, so that you haven’t the shadow of a doubt that you are his and he is yours; but still his left hand isn’t under your head, and his right hand doesn’t embrace you. A shade of sadness has fallen over your heart, perhaps through affliction, certainly through the temporary absence of your Lord. So even while you exclaim, “I am his,” you are forced to go down on your knees and pray, “Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, turn, my Beloved.”

“Where is he?” asks the soul. And the answer comes, “He feedeth among the lilies.” If we want to find Christ, we must get into fellowship with his people; we must come to the ordinances with his saints. Oh, for an evening glimpse of him! Oh, to eat supper with him tonight!

modern: Every sifting comes by *God’s command and permission*. Satan had to ask leave before he could lay a finger on Job. More than that, in a sense our siftings are *the direct work of heaven*, for the text says, “I will sift the house of Israel.” Satan, like a drudge, may hold the sieve, hoping to destroy the grain; but the overruling hand of the Master is making the grain pure by the very process the enemy meant to be destructive. Precious but much-sifted grain on the Lord’s threshing floor, take comfort in the blessed fact that the Lord directs both flail and sieve, to his own glory and to your eternal profit.

The Lord Jesus will surely use the winnowing fan in his hand, and will *separate the precious from the worthless*. Not all who are of Israel are Israel; the heap on the barn floor isn’t all clean grain, and so the winnowing must be done. In the sieve, only true weight counts. Husks and chaff, having no substance, must fly before the wind, and only solid grain will remain.

Notice the *complete safety of the Lord’s wheat*: even the smallest grain has a promise that it will be kept. God himself sifts, and so it is stern and terrible work. He sifts them in every place, “among all nations”; he sifts them in the most thorough way, “like as corn is sifted in a sieve”; and yet, for all this, not the smallest, lightest or most shriveled grain is allowed to fall to the ground. Every single believer is precious in the Lord’s sight. A shepherd wouldn’t lose one sheep, nor a jeweler one diamond, nor a mother one child, nor a man one limb of his body; and the Lord won’t lose one of his redeemed people. However small we may be, if we are the Lord’s, we can rejoice that we are kept safe in Christ Jesus.

modern:
When they heard Jesus’ call, Simon and Andrew obeyed at once, without objection. If we would always put what we hear into practice promptly and with determined zeal, on the spot or at the first fitting chance, our going to the means of grace and our reading of good books couldn’t fail to make us spiritually rich. A man who has taken care to eat his loaf at once won’t lose it, and a man who has already acted on a teaching can’t be robbed of its benefit.

Most readers and hearers are moved far enough to intend to do better, but sadly the intention is a blossom that never sets, and so no fruit comes of it. They wait, they waver, and then they forget, until, like ponds on frosty nights, they thaw when the sun shines by day only to freeze again. That fatal *tomorrow* is blood-red with the murder of good resolutions; it is the slaughterhouse of the innocents.

We are very concerned that our little book of “Evening Readings” shouldn’t be fruitless, and so we pray that readers may not be readers only, but doers of the word. *Practicing the truth is the most profitable way to read it*. If the reader is struck by any duty while reading these pages, let him hurry to do it before the holy glow has left his soul; let him leave his nets and all he has rather than be found rebelling against the Master’s call. Don’t give place to the devil by delay! Hurry while opportunity and the Spirit’s stirring happily come together. Don’t be caught in your own nets, but break the meshes of worldliness and away, where glory calls you.

Happy is the writer who finds readers determined to carry out his teaching! His harvest will be a hundredfold, and his Master will have great honor. I wish to God that such might be our reward for these short meditations and hurried hints. Grant it, O Lord, to your servant!

modern: The whole person of Jesus is like a single gem, and his life is all one impression of the seal. He is altogether complete, not only in each of his parts, but as a gracious, all-glorious whole. His character isn’t a mass of fair colors mixed up in confusion, or a heap of precious stones thrown carelessly on top of each other. He is a picture of beauty and a breastplate of glory. In him all the “things of good repute” are in their proper places, and each helps adorn the others. Not one feature of his glorious person draws attention at the expense of the rest; he is perfectly and altogether lovely.

Oh, Jesus! Your power, your grace, your justice, your tenderness, your truth, your majesty and your unchangeableness make up such a man—or rather such a God-man—as neither heaven nor earth has seen anywhere else. Your infancy, your eternity, your sufferings, your triumphs, your death and your immortality are all woven into one gorgeous tapestry, without seam or tear. You are music without discord; you are many, and yet not divided; you are all things, and yet not scattered. As all the colors blend into one dazzling rainbow, so all the glories of heaven and earth meet in you and unite so wonderfully that there is no one like you in anything. Yes, if all the virtues of the most excellent people were bound in one bundle, they couldn’t rival you, you mirror of all perfection. You have been anointed with the holy oil of myrrh and cassia, which your God has kept for you alone; and as for your fragrance, it is like the holy perfume that no one else may ever mix, even with the perfumer’s art. Each spice is fragrant, but the blend is divine.

modern:
The foundation our faith rests on is this: “God was in Christ reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them.” The great fact that genuine faith relies on is that “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us,” and that “Christ also hath suffered for sin, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God”; “Who himself bare our sins in his own body on the tree”; “For the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed.” In a word, the great pillar of the Christian’s hope is *substitution*. The sacrifice of Christ in the place of the guilty; Christ made sin for us, so that we might be made the righteousness of God in him; Christ offering up a true and real sacrifice that pays for sin, as a substitute in the room, place and stead of all whom the Father gave him, who are known to God by name and are recognized in their own hearts by their trusting in Jesus: this is the central fact of the gospel. If this foundation were removed, what could we do? But it stands as firm as the throne of God. We know it; we rest on it; we rejoice in it; and our delight is to hold it, to meditate on it and to proclaim it, while we long to be driven and moved by gratitude for it in every part of our life and conduct.

In these days a direct attack is being made on the doctrine of the atonement. People can’t bear substitution. They grind their teeth at the thought of the Lamb of God bearing the sin of man. But we who know by experience how precious this truth is will proclaim it in defiance of them, confidently and unceasingly. We will neither water it down nor change it, nor fritter it away in any shape or form. It will still be Christ, a *real substitute*, bearing human guilt and suffering in the place of men. We can’t, we daren’t, give it up, for it is our life; and in spite of every controversy we feel that *“Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure.”*

modern: Christ himself is the builder of his spiritual temple, and he has built it on the mountains of his unchanging love, his almighty grace and his unfailing truthfulness. But as it was in Solomon’s temple, so it is in this one: the materials need to be made ready. There are the “Cedars of Lebanon,” but they aren’t yet framed for the building. They aren’t cut down and shaped and made into those cedar planks whose fragrant beauty will gladden the courts of the Lord’s house in paradise. There are also the rough stones still in the quarry; they must be cut out from there and squared. All this is Christ’s own work. Each believer is being prepared, polished and made ready for his place in the temple, but Christ’s own hand does the preparing. Afflictions can’t make us holy except as he uses them for that purpose. Our prayers and efforts can’t make us ready for heaven apart from the hand of Jesus, who shapes our hearts rightly.

When Solomon’s temple was built, “there was neither hammer, nor axe, nor any tool of iron, heard in the house,” because everything was brought perfectly ready for the exact place it was to fill. So it is with the temple Jesus builds: the making ready is all done on earth. When we reach heaven, there will be no making us holy there, no squaring us with affliction, no planing us with suffering. No, we must be made fit here; Christ will do all *that* beforehand. And when he has done it, a loving hand will ferry us across the river of death and bring us to the heavenly Jerusalem, to stay forever as pillars in the temple of our Lord.

modern:
We have many things in our possession right now that can be shaken, and it doesn’t suit a Christian to set much store by them, for there is nothing stable under these rolling skies; change is written on everything. Yet we have certain “things which *cannot* be shaken,” and I invite you this evening to think about them, so that if the things that can be shaken are all taken away, you may get real comfort from the things that cannot be shaken, which will remain.

Whatever your losses have been or may be, you enjoy present salvation. You are standing at the foot of his cross, trusting only in the merit of Jesus’ precious blood, and no rise or fall of the markets can interfere with your salvation in him. No collapse of banks, no failures and bankruptcies can touch that. Then you are *a child of God* this evening. God is your Father. No change of circumstances can ever rob you of that. Even if losses bring you to poverty and strip you bare, you can say, “He is my Father still. In my Father’s house are many mansions; therefore will I not be troubled.” You have another lasting blessing, namely, *the love of Jesus Christ*. He who is God and Man loves you with all the strength of his affectionate nature, and nothing can affect that. The fig tree may not blossom, and the flocks may vanish from the field; it doesn’t matter to the one who can sing, “My Beloved is mine, and I am his.” We can’t lose our best portion and richest inheritance.

Whatever troubles come, let’s be brave; let’s show that we aren’t such little children as to be cast down by what may happen in this poor, passing life. Our country is Immanuel’s land; our hope is above the sky; and so, as calm as the summer sea, we will watch the wreck of everything born of earth and still rejoice in the God of our salvation.
