modern: A cake that hasn’t been turned is *raw on one side*; and so Ephraim was, in many ways, untouched by God’s grace. Though there was some partial obedience, there was a great deal of rebellion left. My soul, I urge you, see whether this is your case. Are you thorough in the things of God? Has grace gone right through the center of your being, so that its divine work is felt in all your powers, your actions, your words and your thoughts? To be made holy, spirit, soul and body, should be your aim and prayer. And although your sanctification may not be perfect in degree anywhere, it must reach every part. There mustn’t be the appearance of holiness in one place and reigning sin in another, or you too will be a cake not turned.

A cake not turned is *soon burned on the side nearest the fire*. Although no one can have too much true religion, there are some who seem burned black with bigoted zeal for the part of the truth they have received, or charred to a cinder with a proud, Pharisee-like display of the religious practices that suit their taste. A put-on appearance of superior holiness often goes with a total absence of living godliness. The saint in public is a devil in private. He deals in flour by day and in soot by night. The cake that is burned on one side is dough on the other.

*If it is so with me, O Lord, turn me*! Turn my unholy nature to the fire of your love and let it feel the sacred glow; and let my burned side cool a little while I learn my own weakness and lack of heat when I am taken away from your heavenly flame. Don’t let me be found a double-minded man, but one entirely under the powerful influence of reigning grace. For I know well that if I am left like a cake unturned, and not touched by your grace on both sides, I must be consumed forever in everlasting burnings.

modern:
Even in this world the saints are God’s children, but people can’t tell that they are, except by certain marks of character. The adoption hasn’t been made public; the children aren’t yet openly declared. Among the Romans, a man might adopt a child and keep it private for a long time. But there was a second, public adoption, when the child was brought before the proper authorities, its old clothes were taken off, and the father who took it as his child gave it clothes suited to its new station in life. “Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be.” We aren’t yet dressed in the clothes that suit the royal family of heaven. In this flesh and blood we are wearing just what we wore as sons of Adam. But we know that “when *he* shall appear” who is the “first-born among many brethren,” we will be like him, for we will see him as he is.

Can’t you imagine a child taken from the lowest ranks of society and adopted by a Roman senator saying to himself, “I long for the day when I’ll be publicly adopted. Then I’ll take off these common clothes and be dressed as suits my rank as a senator’s son”? Happy in what he has received, he groans for that very reason to have the fullness of what he has been promised. So it is with us today. We are waiting until we can put on our proper clothes and be shown to be the children of God. We are young nobles who haven’t yet worn our coronets. We are young brides, and the wedding day hasn’t come yet; and the love our Bridegroom has for us makes us long and sigh for the wedding morning. Our very happiness makes us groan for more. Our joy, like a swollen spring, longs to well up like an Iceland geyser leaping to the skies, and it heaves and groans within our spirit for lack of room to show itself to the world.

modern:
Some people fondly imagine that being the mother of our Lord must have brought very special privileges, because they suppose she had the benefit of seeing into his very heart in a way we can’t hope to. There may be an appearance of likelihood in the idea, but not much. We don’t know that Mary knew more than others. What she did know, she did well to treasure up in her heart; but from anything we read in the Gospels, she doesn’t appear to have been a better-taught believer than any other of Christ’s disciples. All that she knew, we can discover too.

Are you surprised that we say so? Here is a text to prove it: “The secret of the Lord is with them that fear him, and he will show them his covenant.” Remember the Master’s words: “Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his Lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.” This divine Revealer of secrets tells us his heart so blessedly that he holds back nothing that is good for us. His own assurance is, “If it were not so, I would have told you.” Doesn’t he show himself to us today as he doesn’t to the world? He does. So we won’t cry out in ignorance, “Blessed is the womb that bare thee,” but we will bless God with understanding that, having heard the Word and kept it, we have, first of all, as true a fellowship with the Savior as the Virgin had, and in the second place as true an acquaintance with the secrets of his heart as she can be supposed to have had. Happy soul, to be so privileged!

modern:
The story of the brave courage and marvelous deliverance of the three holy children—or rather, champions—is well suited to stir up in believers firmness and steadiness in holding to the truth in the face of tyranny and in the very jaws of death. Let young Christians especially learn from their example never to sacrifice their consciences, whether in matters of faith or in matters of honesty in business. Lose everything rather than lose your integrity, and when everything else is gone, still hold on to a clear conscience as the rarest jewel that can adorn a mortal’s breast. Don’t be guided by the will-o’-the-wisp of expediency, but by the North Star of God’s authority. Follow the right whatever the risk. When you see no immediate advantage, walk by faith and not by sight. Do God the honor of trusting him when it comes to losing something for the sake of principle. See whether he will stay in your debt! See whether he doesn’t prove his word even in this life, that “Godliness, with contentment, is great gain,” and that those who “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, shall have all these things added unto them.”

If it should happen, in God’s providence, that you lose by keeping your conscience, you will find that if the Lord doesn’t pay you back in the silver of earthly prosperity, he will keep his promise in the gold of spiritual joy. Remember that a man’s life doesn’t consist in the abundance of what he owns. To wear an honest spirit, to have a heart free of offense, to have the favor and smile of God, is greater riches than the mines of Ophir could produce or the trade of Tyre could win. “Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and inward contention therewith.” An ounce of peace of mind is worth a ton of gold.

notes.note: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, Daniel’s friends, thrown into the furnace for refusing to worship Nebuchadnezzar’s golden image ([[Dan.3.17-Dan.3.18|Daniel 3:17–18]]). The old name comes from “The Song of the Three Holy Children,” an addition to Daniel in the Apocrypha.
A will-o’-the-wisp is a flickering light over marshes at night, said to lead travelers astray; policy here means doing whatever seems to pay. The pole-star is the North Star, which sailors steer by.

modern:
Our knowledge of Christ is something like climbing one of our Welsh mountains. When you are at the bottom you see very little; the mountain itself looks only half as high as it really is. Shut in a little valley, you can hardly see anything but the rippling brooks as they run down into the stream at the foot of the mountain. Climb the first rising hillock, and the valley lengthens and widens beneath your feet. Go higher, and you see the country for four or five miles around, and you are delighted with the widening view. Climb further still, and the scene grows larger; until at last, when you are on the summit and look east, west, north and south, you see almost all England lying in front of you. Over there is a forest in some distant county, perhaps two hundred miles away; here is the sea, and there a shining river and the smoking chimneys of a factory town, or the masts of the ships in a busy port. All these things please and delight you, and you say, “I could not have imagined that so much could be seen at this elevation.”

Well, the Christian life is like that. When we first believe in Christ, we see very little of him. The higher we climb, the more of his beauties we discover. But who has ever reached the summit? Who has known all the heights and depths of the love of Christ, which passes knowledge? Paul, grown old, sitting gray-haired and shivering in a dungeon in Rome, could say with more emphasis than we can, “I know whom I have believed,” for every experience had been like climbing a hill, every trial like going up another peak, and his death seemed like reaching the top of the mountain, from which he could see the whole of the faithfulness and love of the one to whom he had committed his soul. Get up, dear friend, into the high mountain.

notes.note: God’s call to Zion to climb high and announce the good news: “Behold your God!” ([[Isa.40.9|Isaiah 40:9]]).

modern:
Reader, can you find rest apart from the ark, Christ Jesus? Then you can be sure your religion is worthless. Are you satisfied with anything less than knowing for yourself that you are joined to Christ and have a share in him? Then woe to you. If you claim to be a Christian, yet find full satisfaction in worldly pleasures and pursuits, your claim is false. If your soul can stretch out at rest, and find the bed long enough and the blanket wide enough to cover her in the rooms of sin, then you are a hypocrite, and far from any right thoughts of Christ or any sense of how precious he is.

But if, on the other hand, you feel that even if you could indulge in sin without punishment, it would be a punishment in itself; and that if you could have the whole world and stay in it forever, it would be misery enough not to be parted from it, because your God—your God—is what your soul craves; then take heart, you are a child of God. With all your sins and imperfections, take this as your comfort: if your soul has no rest in sin, you aren’t as the sinner is! If you are still crying and craving for something better, Christ hasn’t forgotten you, for you haven’t quite forgotten him.

The believer can’t do without his Lord; words can’t express what he thinks of him. We can’t live on the sands of the wilderness; we need the manna that falls from on high. Our leather water bottles of trust in created things can’t give us a drop of moisture, but we drink from the rock that follows us, and that rock is Christ. When you feed on him, your soul can sing, “He hath satisfied my mouth with good things, so that my youth is renewed like the eagle’s.” But if you don’t have him, your overflowing wine vat and well-filled barn can’t give you any satisfaction at all. Mourn over them instead in the words of wisdom: “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity!”

modern:
What must the doom of the professor who falls away be, when his naked soul stands before God? How will he bear that voice: “Depart, ye cursed; you have rejected me, and I reject you; you have played the prostitute and gone away from me; I too have banished you forever from my presence, and will not have mercy on you”? What will this wretch’s shame be on the last great day when, before gathered multitudes, the one who fell away is unmasked? See the godless, and sinners who never claimed any religion, raising themselves from their beds of fire to point at him. “There he is,” says one. “Will he preach the gospel in hell?” “There he is,” says another. “He rebuked me for swearing, and he was a hypocrite himself!” “Aha!” says another. “Here comes a psalm-singing Methodist, one who was always at his chapel. He’s the man who boasted that he was sure of everlasting life, and here he is!” No greater eagerness will ever be seen among the tormentors of hell than on that day when devils drag the hypocrite’s soul down to ruin.

Bunyan pictures this with massive and awful grandeur when he speaks of the back way to hell. Seven devils bound the wretch with nine cords, dragged him from the road to heaven, the road he had claimed to walk, and thrust him through the back door into hell. Watch out for that back way to hell, professors! “Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith.” Look carefully at your condition; see whether you are in Christ or not. It is the easiest thing in the world to give a lenient verdict when you yourself are on trial; but oh, be just and true here. Be just to everyone, but be strict with yourself. Remember, if it isn’t a rock you are building on, when the house falls, great will be its fall. Oh, may the Lord give you sincerity, constancy and firmness; and may you never be led to turn aside, however evil the day.

modern:
Banish forever every thought of indulging the flesh, if you want to live in the power of your risen Lord. It would be wrong for a man who is alive in Christ to live in the rottenness of sin. “Why seek ye the living among the dead?” said the angel to Magdalene. Should the living live in the tomb? Should divine life be walled up in the bone-house of fleshly lust? How can we share the cup of the Lord and still drink the cup of Belial? Surely, believer, you are set free from open lusts and sins. Have you also escaped the more secret and deceptive lime-twigs of the satanic bird-catcher? Have you come out of the lust of pride? Have you escaped from laziness? Have you cleanly escaped from fleshly complacency? Are you trying day by day to live above worldliness, the pride of life and the ensnaring vice of greed? Remember, it is for this that you have been enriched with the treasures of God. If you are really God’s chosen and loved by him, don’t let all the lavish treasure of grace be wasted on you. Pursue holiness; it is the Christian’s crown and glory.

An unholy church! It is useless to the world and of no account among men. It is an abomination, the laughter of hell, the loathing of heaven. The worst evils that have ever come on the world have been brought on her by an unholy church. O Christian, the vows of God are on you. You are God’s priest: act like one. You are God’s king: reign over your lusts. You are God’s chosen: have nothing to do with Belial. Heaven is your portion: live like a heavenly spirit. So you will prove that you have true faith in Jesus, for there can’t be faith in the heart unless there is holiness in the life.

modern:
This is a crafty word from the lips of that arch-tyrant Pharaoh. If the poor enslaved Israelites really must go out of Egypt, then he bargains with them that it won’t be very far: not too far to escape the terror of his armies and the watching of his spies. In the same way, the world doesn’t like nonconformity that really refuses to conform, or dissent that really dissents. It would have us be more easygoing and not handle things too strictly. Death to the world and burial with Christ are experiences that worldly minds ridicule, and so the ordinance that pictures them is almost everywhere neglected, and even condemned. Worldly wisdom recommends the path of compromise and talks of “moderation.” According to this fleshly policy, purity is admitted to be very desirable, but we are warned against being too strict; truth is of course to be followed, but error isn’t to be denounced too severely. “Yes,” says the world, “be spiritually minded by all means, but don’t deny yourself a little lively company, an occasional dance, and a visit to the theater at Christmas. What’s the good of running a thing down when it’s so fashionable and everybody does it?” Multitudes of professors give in to this cunning advice, to their own eternal ruin.

If we want to follow the Lord wholly, we must go right away into the wilderness of separation and leave the Egypt of the fleshly world behind us. We must leave its sayings, its pleasures and its religion too, and go far away to the place where the Lord calls his holy ones. When the town is on fire, our house can’t be too far from the flames. When the plague is about, a man can’t be too far from its haunts. The further from a viper the better, and the further from conforming to the world the better. Let the trumpet call be sounded to all true believers: “Come ye out from among them, be ye separate.”

modern:
Some people have the foolish idea that the only way they can live for God is by becoming ministers, missionaries or Bible women. How many would be shut out from any chance of glorifying the Most High if that were so! Dear friend, it isn’t office but earnestness, it isn’t position but grace, that will enable us to glorify God. God is surely glorified in that cobbler’s stall, where the godly workman sings of the Savior’s love as he works his awl; yes, glorified far more than in many a cathedral stall where official religion goes through its meager duties. The name of Jesus is glorified by the poor, uneducated carter as he drives his horse and blesses his God, or speaks to his fellow worker by the roadside, as much as by the popular preacher who thunders out the gospel up and down the country like Boanerges. God is glorified by our serving him in our proper callings.

Take care, dear reader, that you don’t abandon the path of duty by leaving your occupation, and take care that you don’t dishonor your profession while you are in it. Think little of yourselves, but don’t think too little of your callings. Every lawful trade can be made holy by the gospel for the noblest ends. Turn to the Bible, and you will find the humblest kinds of work connected either with the most daring deeds of faith or with people whose lives were famous for holiness. So don’t be discontented with your calling. Whatever God has made your position or your work, stay in it, unless you are quite sure he calls you to something else. Let your first concern be to glorify God as fully as you can where you are. Fill your present place to his praise, and if he needs you in another, he will show you. This evening, lay aside troublesome ambition and embrace peaceful contentment.

modern:
It is always the Holy Spirit’s work to turn our eyes away from ourselves to Jesus; but Satan’s work is just the opposite, for he is constantly trying to make us look at ourselves instead of Christ. He hints, “Your sins are too great for pardon; you have no faith; you do not repent enough; you will never be able to continue to the end; you have not the joy of his children; you have such a wavering hold of Jesus.” All these are thoughts about self, and we will never find comfort or assurance by looking within. But the Holy Spirit turns our eyes entirely away from self. He tells us that we are nothing, but that “Christ is all in all.”

Remember, then, it isn’t *your hold* on Christ that saves you—it is Christ. It isn’t *your joy* in Christ that saves you—it is Christ. It isn’t even faith in Christ, though that is the means—it is Christ’s blood and merits. So don’t look so much at your hand that is grasping Christ, as at Christ. Don’t look at your hope, but at Jesus, the source of your hope. Don’t look at your faith, but at Jesus, the author and finisher of your faith. We will never find happiness by looking at our prayers, our deeds or our feelings; it is what *Jesus* is, not what we are, that gives rest to the soul. If we want both to overcome Satan and to have peace with God, it must be by “looking unto Jesus.” Keep your eye simply on him. Let his death, his sufferings, his merits, his glories, his pleading for you be fresh in your mind. When you wake up in the morning, look to him; when you lie down at night, look to him. Oh, don’t let your hopes or fears come between you and Jesus. Follow hard after him, and he will never fail you.

notes.note: From Edward Mote’s hymn (1834). A frame is a state of mind or feeling: the singer won’t trust even his happiest mood.

modern:
This incident is an instructive picture of the sure victory of God’s handiwork over all opposition. Whenever a divine principle is planted in the heart, though the devil may make a counterfeit and produce swarms of opponents, as sure as God is in the work, it will swallow up all its enemies. If God’s grace takes possession of a man, the world’s magicians may throw down all their rods, and every rod may be as cunning and poisonous as a serpent, but Aaron’s rod will swallow up their rods. The sweet attractions of the cross will woo and win the man’s heart, and he who lived only for this deceitful earth will now have an eye for the higher spheres and a wing to fly up into heavenly heights. When grace has won the day, the worldly man seeks the world to come.

The same thing can be seen in the believer’s life. What multitudes of enemies our faith has had to meet! Our old sins: the devil threw them down in front of us, and they turned into serpents. What hordes of them! Ah, but the cross of Jesus destroys them all. Faith in Christ makes short work of all our sins. Then the devil sent out another horde of serpents in the form of worldly trials, temptations and unbelief; but faith in Jesus is more than a match for them, and overcomes them all. The same all-consuming principle shines out in faithful service to God! With an eager love for Jesus, difficulties are overcome, sacrifices become pleasures, and sufferings become honors.

But if true religion is a consuming passion in the heart like this, then it follows that many people who claim religion don’t have it, for what they have won’t stand this test. Examine yourself on this point, my reader. Aaron’s rod *proved* its heaven-given power. Is your religion doing that? If Christ is anything, he must be everything. Oh, don’t rest until love for Jesus and faith in him are the ruling passions of your soul!

modern:
Let’s not imagine that *the soul* sleeps unconscious. “Today shalt thou be with me in paradise,” is Christ’s whisper to every dying saint. They “sleep in Jesus,” but their souls are before the throne of God, praising him day and night in his temple, singing hallelujahs to him who washed them from their sins in his blood. It is the body that sleeps in its lonely bed of earth, under its blanket of grass. But what is this sleep? The idea connected with sleep is “*rest*,” and that is the thought the Spirit of God wants to give us. Sleep makes each night a Sabbath for the day. Sleep shuts the door of the soul fast and tells every intruder to wait awhile, so that the life within may enter its summer garden of ease. The toil-worn believer sleeps quietly, as the tired child does when it slumbers at its mother’s breast. Oh, happy are those who die in the Lord! They rest from their labors, and their works follow them. Their quiet rest will never be broken until God wakes them to give them their full reward. Guarded by angel watchers, curtained by eternal mysteries, they sleep on, the heirs of glory, until the fullness of time brings the fullness of redemption.

What an awakening theirs will be! They were laid in their last resting place weary and worn, but they won’t rise like that. They went to their rest with furrowed brows and wasted features, but they wake up in beauty and glory. The shriveled seed, so lacking in shape and beauty, rises from the dust a lovely flower. The winter of the grave gives way to the spring of redemption and the summer of glory. Blessed is death, since by divine power it strips off these working clothes and dresses us in the wedding garment of incorruption. Blessed are those who “sleep in Jesus.”

modern:
Hezekiah was growing so great in his own eyes, and was so proud of God’s favor, that self-righteousness crept in, and because of his careless confidence the grace of God was for a time withdrawn in its more active working. This is quite enough to explain his foolishness with the Babylonians; for if the grace of God were to leave the best Christian, there is sin enough in his heart to make him the worst of sinners. If you were left to yourselves, you who are warmest for Christ would cool down like Laodicea into sickening lukewarmness; you who are sound in the faith would be white with the leprosy of false teaching; you who now walk before the Lord in excellence and integrity would reel back and forth and stagger, drunk with evil passion. Like the moon, we borrow our light. Bright as we are when grace shines on us, we are darkness itself when the Sun of Righteousness withdraws. *So let’s cry to God never to leave us*.

“Lord, don’t take your Holy Spirit from us! Don’t withdraw your indwelling grace from us! Haven’t you said, ‘I the Lord do keep it; I will water it every moment: lest any hurt it, I will keep it night and day’? Lord, keep us everywhere. Keep us when we are in the valley, so that we don’t grumble against your humbling hand. Keep us when we are on the mountain, so that we don’t grow dizzy at being lifted up. Keep us in youth, when our passions are strong. Keep us in old age, when we grow conceited about our wisdom and so may prove bigger fools than the young and giddy. Keep us when we come to die, in case at the very last we should deny you! Keep us living, keep us dying, keep us working, keep us suffering, keep us fighting, keep us resting, keep us everywhere, for everywhere we need you, O our God!”

modern: See the supreme generosity of the Lord Jesus, for he has given us his all. Although a tenth of his possessions would have made a universe of angels rich beyond all imagining, he wasn’t content until he had given us everything he had. It would have been surprising grace if he had let us eat the crumbs of his bounty under the table of his mercy; but he does nothing by halves. He makes us sit with him and share the feast. If he had given us some small pension from his royal treasury, we would have had reason to love him forever; but no, he will have his bride as rich as himself, and he won’t have a glory or a grace that she doesn’t share. He hasn’t been content with anything less than making us joint heirs with himself, so that we might have equal possessions. He has emptied his whole estate into the treasury of the church, and holds everything in common with his redeemed. There isn’t a single room in his house whose key he will keep back from his people. He gives them full freedom to take everything he has as their own. He loves them to make free with his treasure and take as much as they can possibly carry. The boundless fullness of his all-sufficiency is as free to the believer as the air he breathes. Christ has put the flagon of his love and grace to the believer’s lips and told him to drink on forever. If he could drain it, he would be welcome to; and since he can’t exhaust it, he is told to drink deeply, for it is all his own. What truer proof of fellowship can heaven or earth give?

modern:
At the very time when the Chaldeans had surrounded Jerusalem, and the sword, famine and plague had laid the land waste, God commanded Jeremiah to buy a field and have the deed of sale legally sealed and witnessed. This was a strange purchase for a sensible man to make. Prudence couldn’t justify it, for he was buying with hardly any chance that the buyer could ever enjoy the land. But it was enough for Jeremiah that his God had told him to, for he knew well that God will be proved right by all his children. He reasoned like this: “Ah, Lord God! You can make this plot of ground useful to me; you can rid this land of these oppressors; you can still make me sit under my vine and my fig tree in the inheritance I have bought; for you made the heavens and the earth, and there is nothing too hard for you.”

This gave the early saints a certain majesty: they dared to do at God’s command things that mere human reasoning would condemn. Whether it is a Noah who must build a ship on dry land, an Abraham who must offer up his only son, a Moses who must despise the treasures of Egypt, or a Joshua who must besiege Jericho for seven days with no weapons but the blasts of rams’ horns, they all act on God’s command, against the dictates of fleshly reason; and the Lord gives them a rich reward as the result of their obedient faith. I wish to God that the religion of these modern times had a stronger dose of this heroic faith in God. If we would venture more on the bare promise of God, we would enter a world of wonders that we are still strangers to. Let Jeremiah’s place of confidence be ours: nothing is too hard for the God who created the heavens and the earth.

notes.note: The Babylonians, whose army was besieging Jerusalem.

notes.term: Jeremiah was commanded by God to purchase a field
notes.note: While he was in prison and the city was about to fall, Jeremiah bought his cousin’s field as a sign that “houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land” ([[Jer.32.6-Jer.32.15|Jeremiah 32:6–15]]).
